title: The Quantum Adiabatic Theorem for Non-Hermitian Dynamics
authors: G. M. V. S. Aponso, B. P. W. Fernando, K. K. W. A. S. Kumara, R. P. K. De Silva
abstract: We establish a quantitative adiabatic estimate for a class of finite-dimensional non-Hermitian Schrödinger dynamics. The original non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is assumed to be diagonalizable with real spectrum and non-crossing eigenvalues. We then construct a dynamically compatible time-dependent metric operator, and its positive square root defines a Dyson map. The associated Dyson-transformed Hamiltonian is Hermitian.   When this Dyson-transformed Hamiltonian satisfies the Hermitian adiabatic assumption, the standard resolvent-projection method gives an explicit adiabatic estimate in the Hermitian representation. Pulling this estimate back through the Dyson map gives an approximation in the original non-Hermitian representation. The resulting Dyson-pulled-back projections are then compared with the spectral projections of the original non-Hermitian Hamiltonian by using a contour-resolvent estimate. The final bound contains two contributions: the pulled-back Hermitian adiabatic error and the projection-comparison error. A two-level non-Hermitian model is presented to illustrate the hypotheses of the theorem and the two contributions appearing in the final estimate.
summary: This paper develops a quantitative adiabatic theorem for non-Hermitian quantum dynamics by transforming the problem into an equivalent Hermitian system using a Dyson map. It derives an explicit error bound that accounts for both the standard adiabatic approximation error and the additional error introduced by the transformation itself. This provides a powerful theoretical tool for analyzing time evolution in open or dissipative quantum systems.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a rigorous, quantitative adiabatic estimate for quantum systems whose dynamics are governed by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.
main_result: The authors establish an explicit error bound for the adiabatic approximation in non-Hermitian settings by transforming the system into an equivalent Hermitian representation and quantifying the transformation error.
method: The method involves constructing a dynamically compatible Dyson map using a metric operator to transform the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}_T$) into a Hermitian counterpart ($ ar{H}_T$). The standard adiabatic theorem is then applied in this transformed space, with errors quantified via contour-resolvent estimates.
model_or_system: The analysis applies to finite-dimensional quantum systems evolving under time-dependent, non-Hermitian Schrödinger dynamics. A two-level model is used to illustrate the full scope of the theorem and its error components.
key_observables: The final estimate controls the evolution operator error $|e^{U_{A, \pm}(s)} - \hat{U}_T(s)|$, and the analysis tracks spectral projections and gap sizes in the transformed Hermitian system.
important_parameters: The time parameter $s$ (ranging from 0 to 1), the spectral gap of the effective Hermitian Hamiltonian $ ar{H}_T(s)$, and the adiabatic constant $T$.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include that the original non-Hermitian Hamiltonian must be diagonalizable with a real spectrum, possess non-crossing eigenvalues, and satisfy a contour-resolvent condition for the transformed system.
figures_summary: The notes do not describe specific figures, but mention the final estimate containing two explicit error contributions: the pulled-back Hermitian adiabatic error and the projection-comparison error, illustrated by the two-level model.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the need for an adiabatic theorem extension to non-Hermitian dynamics. It then introduces the Dyson map construction to achieve a Hermitian representation ($ ar{H}_T$). Finally, it applies standard adiabatic techniques in this transformed space and pulls the resulting estimate back to yield the final bound.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for AMO physics and open quantum systems because non-Hermiticity naturally arises when coupling quantum systems to an environment or when considering gain/loss processes. Providing a rigorous adiabatic framework for these dynamics is crucial for modeling physical reality beyond simple unitary evolution.
